source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: The most copied LLM memory ranker. Each memory is scored on recency, importance and relevance, each min-max scaled to 0-1, then summed. It is ACT-R-like but not ACT-R.
numbers: Recency = exponential decay, factor 0.995 per sandbox hour since last retrieval. Importance = LLM rates 1 to 10. Relevance = cosine of embeddings. All three weights set to 1. Top memories that fit the context window go in the prompt.
limits: No use-count (frequency) term, which ACT-R has. Decay is exponential, not power law. Weights never tuned.
agent_relevance: Start from this ranker, then add use-count and a power-law decay term and test each.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: Ablation of whole components: removing memory access, reflection or planning lowers how believable the agents' interview answers are. The full architecture ranked best.
numbers: TrueSkill mu: no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; human crowdworkers 22.95; no memory, planning or reflection 21.21. Full vs fully ablated Cohen d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis H(4) = 150.29, p < 0.001. 100 evaluators.
limits: Ablations remove observation, reflection and planning, not the three retrieval terms. So it does not show each retrieval term matters. Full-architecture mu not re-read here.
agent_relevance: Shows memory plus reflection helps. It does not validate the ranking formula itself.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) MemoryBank: Enhancing Large Language Models with Long-Term Memory
finding: Uses an Ebbinghaus-style forgetting curve to update memory strength. Each recall resets the curve. Tested in the SiliconFriend chatbot on ChatGLM, BELLE and ChatGPT.
numbers: Retention R = e^(-t/S), S grows with each recall. English retrieval accuracy: ChatGLM 0.809, BELLE 0.814, ChatGPT 0.763. Chinese: 0.84, 0.856, 0.711. English correctness: 0.438, 0.479, 0.716.
limits: Exponential, not power law. The table read gives no ablation of the forgetting step. Small hand-built test set.
agent_relevance: A cheap recall-strengthens-memory rule exists, but the evidence that the forgetting step helps is thin.

source: Hou et al. (2024) My agent understands me better: dynamic human-like memory recall and consolidation in LLM agents
finding: Adds a recall-count-dependent decay: each recall slows later forgetting. Compared with Generative Agents scoring on 10 recall tasks.
numbers: Recall probability p(t) = (1 - exp(-r e^(-t/g))) / (1 - e^-1). Recall trigger threshold 0.86, set by trials. Paired t = -5.687, p = 0.000299, critical t 2.26, 95% CI of loss difference [-0.27, -0.12]. 10 tasks with 4 candidate events each. Also 6 participants over 1 week to 3 months, qualitative only.
limits: Tiny task set built by the same team. Metric is softmax loss for picking the right event. Threshold is ad hoc. Not ACT-R's sum of power-law traces.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM-agent analogue of ACT-R use-history. The effect is promising but the test is weak.

source: Sumers et al. (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Framework mapping language agents onto memory types and a decision loop. It discusses Soar at length. The extracted text has no mention of ACT-R.
numbers: Count of 'ACT-R' in extracted text: 0. Soar has its own figure.
limits: Survey with no experiments. Says nothing about activation-based ranking.
agent_relevance: Activation-based memory ranking is an open design option for language agents, not an established one.

source: Yuan, Su, Yao (2026) Diagnosing retrieval vs utilization bottlenecks in LLM agent memory (ICLR 2026)
finding: On LoCoMo the retrieval method matters more than how memories are written. Raw chunks (zero LLM calls) match or beat extracted facts and summaries.
numbers: 3x3 grid, 1,540 non-adversarial questions, k = 5. Accuracy by retrieval method (averaged over write strategies): BM25 57.1%, cosine 73.4%, hybrid with LLM rerank 77.2%. Write strategies differ only 3 to 8 points. Raw chunks: 77.9% cosine, 81.1% hybrid. Retrieval failures 11 to 46% of questions; BM25 with extracted facts 46.3%.
limits: No recency, frequency or activation term tested. The reranker is an LLM judge (GPT-5.2), so costly. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Ranking is where gains are. Any ACT-R-style term must be tested against a strong hybrid ranker.

source: SYNAPSE (2026) Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Agent memory graph with ACT-R-style spreading activation, fan dilution, temporal node decay and lateral inhibition. Beats 10 memory baselines on LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini.
numbers: Weighted F1 (excluding adversarial) 40.5 vs A-Mem 33.3 (+7.2), Zep 39.7, MemoryOS 38.0, LangMem 34.3. Temporal F1 50.1 vs A-Mem 45.9. Settings: spreading S = 0.8, decay 0.01, 384-dim embeddings. About 814 tokens per query vs about 16.9K for full LoCoMo context.
limits: Own equations inspired by ACT-R, not an ACT-R implementation. Adversarial 96.6 F1 relies on a rejection gate. One benchmark and backbone in the main table.
agent_relevance: ACT-R-style dynamics can lift LLM memory. The ablation says which parts earn it.

source: SYNAPSE (2026) ablation table
finding: Node decay alone drives temporal questions. Fan effect drives open-domain and multi-hop questions.
numbers: Full: multi-hop 35.7, temporal 50.1, open 25.9, single 48.9, adversarial 96.6, average 40.5. No node decay: temporal 14.2, average 30.7. No fan effect: open 16.8, multi-hop 30.2, average 36.1. No lateral inhibition: adversarial 71.5. No activation dynamics: average 30.5. Vectors only: average 25.2, temporal 14.7.
limits: Authors' own ablation. LoCoMo temporal questions favor newer facts by design, so the decay gain may be benchmark-specific.
agent_relevance: Decay and fan are the ACT-R parts with measured value. Keep these two first.

source: FadeMem (2026) Biologically-Inspired Forgetting for Efficient Agent Memory
finding: Two-layer memory with decay rates set by importance, relevance, access frequency and recency. Cuts storage by 45% while keeping retrieval quality.
numbers: Retained 82.1% of critical facts at 55.0% storage vs Mem0 78.4% at 100%, MemGPT 75.6% at 85.3%. LoCoMo multi-hop F1 29.43 vs Mem0 28.37, MemGPT 9.46. MSC RP@10 77.2% vs Mem0 74.8%. Dropping the dual layer cut multi-hop F1 from 29.43 to 19.45; dropping fusion cut it to 13.63. Conflict-resolution consistency 80.4% on LTI-Bench.
limits: Not ACT-R. Decay is mostly importance-driven with a saturating frequency term. Ablations remove architecture parts, not the frequency term alone.
agent_relevance: Frequency inside decay is plausible but not isolated here.

source: CAMeR (2026) Keyword-Gated Hybrid Activation for Adaptive Memory Retention in LLM Agents
finding: Decay with reinforcement on use. The keyword gate, not learned decay, drives results. LoCoMo cannot test retention because every query touches every memory.
numbers: Fixed decay 0.99 per round, reinforcement +0.2; 0.99^100 = 0.366. On LoCoMo's 19 session summaries all weights saturated at 0.99 or higher. Top-5 retrieval saves 83.2% tokens (39k vs 231k). On its own 76-memory, 100-round benchmark the gate gives a 1.6x larger retention gap between high-frequency and never-referenced memories.
limits: Own tiny synthetic benchmark. A learned per-memory decay (81-parameter MLP) did not beat the gate.
agent_relevance: Use-count reinforcement saturates if every query activates everything. Needs a retrieval threshold, as in ACT-R.

source: OBLIVION (2026) Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation
finding: Forgetting as falling accessibility, not deletion. Decay with reinforcement from use. An uncertainty gate decides when to read memory. Large token savings.
numbers: LongMemEval (S), GPT-4.1-mini: best config 90.60% vs direct retrieval baseline 89.00%. Up to 73% token-cost reduction at 120K interaction spans. Decay temperature T = 10 balanced; T = 1 and 3 gave near-zero retention; T = 50 saturated the buffer and recreated always-on retrieval. GoodAI LTM (2K) normalized score 8.41 for full hierarchy vs 6.00 for L3-only.
limits: Accuracy gain is small (1.6 points). The win is cost. Best T depends on buffer size. Ebbinghaus exponential, not ACT-R power law.
agent_relevance: Decay rate must match buffer size. Too slow equals no forgetting.

source: Moscati et al. and Reiter-Haas et al. (as summarised in the PISA paper) ACT-R for music relistening
finding: Earlier work used ACT-R base-level and spreading terms to predict relistening, and for hashtag reuse, app usage, job and genre preference. Pure ACT-R only recommends items already used, so Moscati added collaborative filtering.
numbers: Claim in PISA related work: ACT-R memory module beat baselines that pick recent songs. Numbers not read here.
limits: Secondhand through PISA's related work.
agent_relevance: Pure activation ranking finds old items but cannot find new ones. Our agent needs a separate exploration path.

source: PISA (2024) Transformers Meet ACT-R: Repeat-Aware and Sequential Listening Session Recommendation
finding: Puts ACT-R base-level (time-decayed sum over past listens) and spreading terms into a Transformer. Best on 10 of 12 NDCG and Recall metrics, beating ACT-R-only baselines.
numbers: Last.fm NDCG: PISA-P 12.16%, PISA-U 12.09%. Deezer NDCG: PISA-P 11.20%, PISA-U 10.27%. True repeat share in test sessions: 72.37% Last.fm, 89.10% Deezer. Frequency-only P-Top: repetition NDCG 12.33 but exploration NDCG 0.07. Mean over 5 runs.
limits: Music, not text memory. Authors note ACT-R baselines focused on relisten prediction or explainability, not accuracy. Per-row values of ACT-R baselines not recoverable from the extracted table.
agent_relevance: Frequency and recency win on repeats and fail on novelty. Pair activation with a novelty route.

source: Honda et al. (2025) ACT-R base-level activation with cosine similarity for LLM agent memory (HAI '25)
finding: Reported only in a web-search summary: combines ACT-R base-level activation with cosine similarity for LLM agent memory retrieval.
numbers: Not read. No numbers.
limits: Paper not found or opened this session.
agent_relevance: Follow up before citing.

source: Meghdadi, Duff, Demberg (2026) Integrating language model embeddings into the ACT-R cognitive modeling framework
finding: Replaces ACT-R's hand-set association strengths with Word2Vec or BERT cosine similarity, plus a fan penalty from the 20 nearest neighbours. Predicts priming reaction times.
numbers: Semantic Priming Project, 200 ms SOA, 6,641 prime-target pairs, 512 participants. Best model (Word2Vec + frequency + visual + fan) Spearman rho 0.51, CI 0.49 to 0.53, RMSE 75.97 ms. BERT version 0.50. Similarity alone 0.20 to 0.21. Frequency alone 0.42. Plain linear regression 0.51. Gemma-2B and LLM2Vec did not beat BERT.
limits: Does not beat linear regression. Spreading alone predicts poorly. Only one SOA in main text. Page read to character 100,000 of 125,214.
agent_relevance: Embedding similarity works as the spreading term but adds little beyond frequency. Supports a simple recency and frequency core.

source: Stocco et al. (2024) Fitting, Evaluating, and Comparing Cognitive Architecture Models Using Likelihood: A Primer With Examples in ACT-R
finding: Primer on maximum likelihood, AIC and BIC for ACT-R models. States the declarative activation equation and the parameters that matter.
numbers: A_t(c) = log sum (t - t_i)^(-d). Declarative parameters: decay d (:BLL) affects accuracy and RT; activation noise s (:ANS) affects accuracy and RT; latency factor F (:LF) affects RT only.
limits: Methods paper, no new memory data. Says architecture models rarely use likelihood-based comparison.
agent_relevance: Tells us which parameters to log and fit (d and noise) if we want a measured memory ranker.

source: Georgiou, Katkov, Can, Tsodyks (2023) Large-scale study of human memory for meaningful narratives
finding: LLMs were used to build and score human narrative-recall experiments. Recall scales linearly with narrative length. Stories show no primacy effect, unlike random word lists.
numbers: Recall and recognition scale linearly with narrative length. Scrambled narratives cut recall but recognition stayed largely unaffected. An LLM-embedding measure of clause similarity to the whole narrative correlates strongly with recall probability. Word-list recall follows power laws with primacy and recency.
limits: Participant counts not extracted. Human memory for meaningful text depends on gist fit, not only on access history.
agent_relevance: For rich text, relevance to the whole context matters beside recency. Keep a semantic term.

source: Ji-An et al. (2024) Linking in-context learning in transformers to human episodic memory
finding: Induction heads in LLMs behave like the CMR model of human episodic memory, with contiguity and forward asymmetry. Ablating CMR-like heads hurts in-context learning.
numbers: Ablating the top 10% CMR-like heads gave worse in-context-learning scores than ablating the same number of random heads in most models tested.
limits: Compares to CMR, not ACT-R. About memory inside the model, not an external store.
agent_relevance: Models already show temporal contiguity internally. An external recency term may partly duplicate it.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) EM-LLM: Human-inspired Episodic Memory for Infinite Context LLMs
finding: Splits context into events by surprise. Retrieves by similarity plus temporal contiguity and asymmetry. Beats RAG and full context on long-context tests.
numbers: Beats NV-Embed-v2 RAG by 30.5% on LongBench and 11.5% on InfiniteBench (paper's relative figures). Best on 80% of LongBench task groups. Up to 40% and 29.7% gain over InfLLM on some multi-document tasks.
limits: Uses contiguity (CMR), not ACT-R activation. Works on the KV cache, not a text memory.
agent_relevance: Fetching neighbours of a hit is a cheap alternative to ACT-R's frequency term.

source: Cognitive LLMs / LLM-ACTR (2024) Integrating cognitive architectures and LLMs for manufacturing decision-making
finding: Fine-tunes Llama with ACT-R model representations to predict human-like decisions in a manufacturing task. The ACT-R part is mostly production utility learning, not declarative memory.
numbers: Held-out accuracy 0.6576 (NLL 0.6534) vs Llama alone 0.3564 (NLL 1.133) and chance 0.4826. Single-facet target accuracy 0.64, multi-facet 0.42. Concatenating embeddings gave 0.71 for both variants, no gain.
limits: Procedural, not declarative. Simulated ACT-R personas, not people. Needs fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: ACT-R traces can steer an LLM, but only with training, which our scaffold avoids.

source: Hybrid Personalization Using Declarative and Procedural Memory Modules of the Cognitive Architecture ACT-R (UMAP '25)
finding: Position paper. Recommender chunks get activation from base-level (recency, frequency) plus spreading. Production rules re-weight them and give explanations.
numbers: No experiments, no numbers.
limits: Proposal only.
agent_relevance: Rule-based re-weighting of memory scores is traceable, matching our need to log why a memory was used.

source: pensyve-core activation.rs (open-source agent memory library)
finding: Per a search summary, implements ACT-R B = ln(sum (t - t_k)^-d) with default d = 0.5. A second project replaces symbolic spreading with embedding overlap.
numbers: d = 0.5 default (secondhand).
limits: Not opened. Code, not research.
agent_relevance: Practitioners adopt d = 0.5 untested.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Founding rational analysis. The need for an item in real text and mail follows power laws of recency and frequency, matching human forgetting.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened; from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Supports power-law over exponential decay in our memory.

source: Pavlik & Anderson (2005) Practice and forgetting effects on vocabulary memory
finding: Activation model with spacing-dependent decay fit human vocabulary learning better than fixed-decay models.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened; from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Decay should depend on spacing, which Hou et al. approximate for LLMs.

source: Hou et al. (2024) failure case, Task 0
finding: Both the decay model and the Generative Agents scorer chose the wrong event on one task. The decay model leaned on relevance and short elapsed time; the other leaned on recency and importance.
numbers: 1 of 10 tasks failed by both models. Paper gives per-event relevance, elapsed time and score columns but no aggregate accuracy.
limits: Reported as an example, not a failure rate analysis. Paper reports loss, not accuracy percent.
agent_relevance: Different ranking formulas fail on different items. Log the score parts per retrieval to diagnose misses.
